newsitem.title: UK: Belgian scientist "accidentally cloned" baby, paper says.
newsitem.headline: Belgian scientist "accidentally cloned" baby, paper says.

text.p: A Belgian doctor may have accidentally created the first human "clone", a British newspaper reported on Sunday.
The unidentified four-year-old boy living in Belgium was the result of a technique developed to improve the success rate of fertility treatment, the Sunday Times said.

The news follows blanket coverage last week in Britain of a forecast by the scientists who created Dolly the sheep, the world's first adult clone, that human cloning could be a reality in one or two years if scientists wanted to do it.
The child, who lives with his parents and identical twin brother in southern Belgium, was created after scientists took a frozen fertilised egg and rubbed its surface with a glass rod.
The technique is designed to improve the chances of the egg's implantation in the mother's womb.
But the scientists were astounded to discover three weeks later that the egg had developed into two embryos.

"Although this division can occur naturally, producing identical twins, doctors involved say that the rubbing technique thinned the outer wall of the egg, encouraging it to divide," the newspaper reported.

Martine Nijs, a biologist at the Van Helmont hospital near Brussels, developed the rubbing technique and reported her findings in a scientific journal. But the information was not publicised outside medical circles.

"It was cloning by accident," Nijs told the newspaper. "You can imagine how excited we were when after 25 days we could tell by the foetal heartbeat that it was twins." But Nijs was cautious about whether the technique would be used intentionally for cloning.

"Our hospital ethics committee wouldn't necessarily oppose it. If someone asks us to do it, we would have to say we could not guarantee to create identical twins," Nijs said. The newspaper said there was no legal ban on human cloning in Belgium, unlike Britain.
Cloning, which creates genetically identical individuals, can be done by splitting embryos or by transferring the nucleus of one cell into an egg -- the technique used for Dolly.
The news that Dolly the sheep had been cloned using a cell from an adult sheep prompted a flurry of soul-searching last week about whether the technology was morally acceptable.
U.S. President Bill Clinton banned federal funding of cloning and German Research Minister Juergen Ruettgers called for a worldwide ban on cloning human beings.

But Ian Wilmut, the chief scientist at Scotland's Roslin Institute where the Dolly experiment was carried out, told a parliamentary committee last week there was no scientific reason why similar techniques could not be developed for humans.

"If you really wanted to do it it could be done," he said. But Wilmut said work with human eggs would be "offensive". "We could see no clinical reason why you would wish to make a copy of a person," he told a parliamentary committee.
"We are pleased that it is already illegal in this country so we would support wholeheartedly the idea of (international) prohibition in as effective a way as possible," Wilmut said.
